item.title: 🟠 The developer laptop just became production. Now what?
item.description:

For decades, enterprise software development relied on an assumption that developers could experiment relatively safely because there were safeguards between their work and production. Development, staging and production had different rules, with human intermediaries making judgments about what was ready to move forward. Testing also assumed that software would behave predictably when executed again.

Coding agents are upending both assumptions. Developers now run autonomous software on laptops containing GitHub tokens, SSH keys, cloud credentials and authenticated browser sessions. They’re connecting agents to MCP servers, granting access to repositories and services, and copying suggested commands into terminals without always understanding what those commands will do. item.title: 🟠 Jev and the era of model Tetris
item.description:
Why this matters: Could affect sign-ins, MFA, or Conditional Access — watch for authentication issues.

This spring, in an interview after a keynote, I said we were all playing LLM Tetris now. The days of using the same LLM for every agent problem were over. Some decisions needed to come back in milliseconds, and some could take three minutes. Some needed generative output, and some needed logical decisions where an open-weight model might do. Fit the model to the use case.

I still believe that. But I was only half right, because I was still picturing every piece as an LLM. Bigger or smaller, pricier or cheaper, faster or slower, but all the same shape: text in, text out.

On September 15, a model shipped that doesn’t write anything. Within three weeks, more than a dozen others followed, from OpenAI, Cloudflare and Perplexity to open-source projects you can run on a laptop. Then on October 27, we got yet another class of model from Liquid AI, small enough to run on a phone.

The game I described in the spring is real. It just has more piece shapes than I expected, and it isn’t only an LLM game anymore. It’s model Tetris now.

item.title: 🔴 Why does old access outlive the job?
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

Old access persists beyond its intended purpose and most organizations never monitor it. New access rights arrive within a day of a request. Old rights get revoked, if they get revoked at all, only upon prompting someone. Tools that assist employees in confirming, rotating and vaulting their service accounts have taught me again and again that removing access has to be as thoughtful as granting access. Security professionals can bridge this chasm with simple changes to their policies for role moves and access reviews.

This happens all the time. An employee moves from one team to another. The new manager approves the access needed for the new role within a day, and the person is productive by lunch. The access from the old role stays. After months, access review has one query only: “Do you still need it?” The reviewer sees the name next to the entitlement, but nothing on the dashboard shows whether it has been used since the move. item.description:

Microsoft researchers have uncovered a memory-safety bug in Rust’s standard library that had gone undetected for nearly 11 years, alongside other flaws that can trigger undefined behavior even in applications written entirely in safe Rust. Two of the findings affect stable Rust, including a separate issue that could cause applications to access freed memory.

The nearly 11-year-old bug involves Rust’s process::exit function. Microsoft’s FORGE Lab researchers found that calling the function from a child thread could cause the runtime to remove the main thread’s alternate signal stack while it was still running. If the main thread subsequently experienced a stack overflow, the operating system could be unable to deliver the signal correctly, resulting in a segmentation fault instead of Rust’s intended stack-overflow handling.
